key: But the LORD was wroth with me for your sakes, and hearkened not unto me; and the LORD said unto me: ‘Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto Me of this matter.
s: Moses recalls pleading to cross the Jordan into the good land; Rashi, on 3:26, reads ‘Let it suffice’ as ending the plea lest people call the master harsh and the disciple importunate, or as telling him much more is stored up for him.
src: Rashi, Commentary on the Torah, on Deuteronomy 3:26, Rosenbaum and Silbermann’s Hebrew text (1929 to 1934), Sefaria export 3f10136 (2026)

evidence.words: רב לך. שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמְרוּ הָרַב כַּמָּה קָשֶׁה וְהַתַּלְמִיד כַּמָּה סַרְבָן וּמַפְצִיר (סוטה י"ג); דָּ"אַ — רב לך, הַרְבֵּה מִזֶּה שָׁמוּר לְךָ, רַב טוּב הַצָּפוּן לְךָ (ספרי)
evidence.gloss: [Rashi on 3:26, ‘Let it suffice thee’:] So that they should not say: how harsh is the Master and how obstinate and importunate the disciple (Sotah 13). Another explanation: ‘rav lekha’, much more than this is kept for you, abundant good is stored up for you (Sifrei).

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref and at match). Plain sense faithful to 3:23 to 25, where Moses recalls asking to cross over. Rashi on 3:26, ‘rav lekha’, gives exactly the two explanations the sentence names: lest people say the Master is harsh and the disciple importunate (Sotah 13), and, another explanation, that much good is stored up for him (Sifrei). No drift; only three words of the key verse quoted. entry-check ok.
